false_positives.candidate:
New sorted-set operations are incompatible with existing Redis segment keys

Existing span-buf:s:* keys created before this change are Redis sets, but process_spans now issues ZADD against them and the Lua script and _load_segment_data use ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN. Redis will return WRONGTYPE for those keys, so batches for traces active during deployment can fail until the keys expire after redis_ttl (3600s), and mixed old/new consumers during rollout will break each other. No key-version bump, conversion, or fallback is provided.

ZUNIONSTORE sums duplicate span scores instead of preserving timestamps

Both merge sites call ZUNIONSTORE without an AGGREGATE clause, so Redis defaults to SUM. When the same payload exists in both the destination and source sorted sets (e.g. duplicate delivery or a span stored under two keys before redirects converge), its score becomes roughly twice its end_timestamp_precise. That corrupts the ordering later used by ZPOPMIN eviction, causing duplicated spans to be retained while unrelated spans are evicted. The merge should use AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN) to preserve a real timestamp.

Insert-time eviction silently flushes incomplete segments as if complete

When a segment exceeds a hard-coded 1000 spans, ZPOPMIN discards the lowest end_timestamp_precise spans with no metric, log, or marker on the flushed segment. Those spans are permanently lost, yet flush_segments will emit the remainder as a normal segment (and the has-root flag/queue timeout may already have been set, so it flushes on the short root timeout). This replaces the previous explicit too-large-segment handling with silent partial data, ignores the configurable SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (default 1001), and with tied scores eviction order is lexicographic by payload, so even a needed span can be dropped arbitrarily.

Redirect chain resolution regresses from 10000 to 1000 hops

The loop that follows span-buf:sr redirects was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations, removing the comment that explained the 10k limit. Segment trees whose parent chain needs more than 1000 redirect hops will stop at an intermediate span ID, so later spans are merged into the wrong set and the trace is flushed as multiple split segments instead of one segment. No test or justification covers chains between 1000 and 10000 hops.

Flush-time max_segment_spans protection was removed without an equivalent guard

_load_segment_data no longer checks len(payloads[key]) against self.max_segment_spans, drops the segment_span_count_exceeded metric/log, and returns arbitrarily large segments as long as they stay under the byte limit. Segments created before the Lua eviction existed, created by mixed-version workers, or built under a different configured limit will now be loaded and produced downstream regardless of the configured span cap, risking oversized Kafka messages and memory pressure during flush.

process_batch now crashes the whole batch if end_timestamp_precise is absent

Span construction changed from tolerating minimal span payloads to requiring val["end_timestamp_precise"] via direct indexing; the cast to SpanEvent is typing-only and does not validate the runtime JSON. A single older or malformed message missing that field raises KeyError, aborting process_batch for every span in the batch and causing the same batch to be retried instead of only the bad message being dropped or defaulted.

No tests cover eviction, score merging, or the new paginator path

The added/updated tests only supply end_timestamp_precise for existing small-segment scenarios. Nothing inserts more than 1000 spans into one segment to verify how many and which spans survive ZPOPMIN, whether the root span is retained, or how duplicate payloads merged by ZUNIONSTORE keep their scores, and there are no tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator against a datetime-ordered queryset or for negative cursors. The riskiest new behaviors in this change are therefore unverified.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision uses the outer dataset instead of the dataset actually queried

_get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset and executes the query against it, but is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects is called with the closure variable dataset. The dashboard-split factory calls _get_event_stats with discover or another split_dataset that can differ from the original dataset, so an errors split query can be denied upsampling because the outer dataset was metrics/transactions-like, or upsampling can be considered based on a dataset different from the one that will run the query.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: the upsampling eligibility check (`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`) is passed the outer `dataset` closure variable instead of the `scoped_dataset` parameter, which breaks upsampling decisions in dashboard-split scenarios where `scoped_dataset` is `discover` while the outer `dataset` is `metrics`.

false_positives.candidate:
Upsampling cache can return stale or colliding eligibility results

Eligibility is cached for 60 seconds under a key containing only organization ID and hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))). The defined invalidate_upsampling_cache helper is never called when the project allowlist option changes, so projects removed from the allowlist can continue to be overcounted and newly added projects can continue to be undercounted until expiry; a hash collision between different project sets would also reuse the wrong eligibility. The TTL can additionally expire between the multiple _get_event_stats calls made by the dashboard-split flow, producing inconsistent transformations within one request.

Substring event.type check misclassifies discover queries in both directions

_is_error_focused_query only searches request.GET['query'] for the substring 'event.type:error'. A negated query such as '!event.type:error' therefore returns True and applies sum(sample_weight) to non-error events, while valid error-focused forms such as '!event.type:transaction', 'event.type:[error,default]', or the errors-only split query constructed by the endpoint ('(<query>) AND !event.type:transaction') return False because the helper also ignores the actual query argument passed to _get_event_stats. This causes overcounting for excluded-error queries and missed upsampling for legitimate error queries.

upsampled_count has no fallback for events without sample_weight

The aggregate is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)), replacing a row count that counted every event. Any stored error row whose sample_weight is null or 0 (for example events ingested before client sampling was enabled/configured for an allowlisted project, or events without a client_sample_rate) contributes 0 instead of 1, so historical or unsampled buckets in the retention window can drop to zero or be undercounted after the transformation. The added tests only cover events explicitly given client_sample_rate through the new factory helper.

upsampled_count is exposed as a public Discover function

The new SnQLFunction does not set private=True, unlike internal-only aggregates, so it becomes user-callable through the Discover query builder. A caller can submit upsampled_count() directly as a yAxis/field for projects and datasets that never passed the organization-events-stats allowlist and dataset checks, bypassing the gating in error_upsampling.py and receiving raw sum(sample_weight) results (including misleading zero values for transaction data).

Accidental git submodule added to the repository root

This new file adds 'Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a' as a submodule named sentry-repo at the repository root. It is unrelated to the upsampling feature and will change checkout/CI behavior for every developer by introducing a nested Sentry checkout; it should be removed before merging.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every distinct cache-negative Check now issues a fresh permissions DB query

When cached permissions do not allow the request, Check unconditionally calls getIdentityPermissions, and getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions no longer consult permCache before querying permissionStore. The denial cache is per user+action+name+parent, so it only suppresses repeats for the exact same resource. Checking N different dashboards/folders a user cannot access (e.g. an authorizer evaluating many objects, or a client probing/enumerating UIDs) therefore causes N sequential SQL permission queries for the same user/action, even though the scope map was already fetched and refreshed by the first query; singleflight only coalesces concurrent identical calls. This defeats the 30s permission cache for denial-heavy workloads and amplifies DB load proportional to distinct resource names.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the exact same code behavior in the Check operation: cached permission grants are trusted immediately, while cache misses/denials bypass the permission cache and trigger a fresh database lookup. However, the Golden Comment frames this asymmetry as a security risk (stale grants should not be trusted if denials aren't), whereas the Candidate Issue frames it as a performance/DB load issue (denials should use the permission cache to avoid N database queries). Because they identify the exact same underlying code mechanism and anomaly (asymmetric handling of cached grants vs denials in Check), there is a strong overlap in the code issue identified, though the security conclusion is missed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial key uses raw subject identifier and ambiguous underscore concatenation

permDenialKey is built from checkReq.UserUID, the raw identifier parsed from the subject, whereas permCache is keyed by the canonical UID returned by GetUserIdentifiers. The same person addressed as user:<numeric-id> versus user:<uid> therefore gets separate denial entries and inconsistent fast-path behaviour. Additionally userPermDenialCacheKey joins action, name and parent with '_' without escaping, so pairs such as (name='a_b', parent='c') and (name='a', parent='b_c') produce the same key and one resource's denial can incorrectly deny the other for that user.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same problem described in the golden comment: `userPermDenialCacheKey` joins components with an underscore without escaping, leading to key collisions and incorrect denial cache hits. Although the candidate also mentions an additional issue regarding the raw subject identifier, it fully covers the golden comment's concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key does not include identity type

userPermDenialCacheKey is built only from namespace, the raw subject identifier, action, name and parent. Anonymous subjects (anonymous:0) and the render service (render:0) both have identifier "0", and user/service-account identifiers can also overlap. If an anonymous check for dashboards:read on dash1 is denied and cached, a subsequent render-service check for the same action/name/parent hits that denial at service.go:117 and returns Allowed=false, even though getRendererPermissions grants the renderer read access to all dashboards/folders. Different identity types must not share denial entries; include the identity type (or identity-specific prefixes like the permission cache uses) in the key.

Cached denial blocks access immediately after a grant or resource creation

Any DB-confirmed denial is stored in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30s), and lines 116-121 return that denial without re-querying permissions. If the denied check happened just before the resource was created or before a permission/role was granted for that same name/parent (a common pre-creation or permission-assignment flow), the creator/grantee is still denied for up to 30s, which is exactly the newly-created dashboard/folder scenario this PR aims to fix. The denial timestamp also starts after the underlying permission/team/role caches were populated, so it can extend staleness beyond their expiry.

List still serves stale cached permissions, so newly created resources do not appear

List returns getCachedIdentityPermissions whenever the cache lookup succeeds, with no revalidation, freshness check, or DB fallback. If a user creates a dashboard/folder (adding a permission not present in the cached scope map) and then lists dashboards/folders within the 30s permCache TTL, the new resource is omitted from the List response even though a Check for that same resource would now re-query the DB and allow it. This leaves Check and List inconsistent and does not fully deliver the stated goal of letting users fetch newly created dashboards/folders.

DB fallback does not refresh team, basic-role or folder-tree caches before caching a denial

The fallback at lines 139-155 re-queries only the permission rows: getUserPermissions still obtains basic role and team memberships from basicRoleCache/teamCache, and the second checkPermission still obtains ancestors from the cached folderCache via buildFolderTree. If access should be granted because of a recent team/role change or via a newly created intermediate folder, the fallback still evaluates with the stale role/team/folder-tree data, returns false, and then writes a fresh 30s denial entry, extending the incorrect denial beyond the expiry of those underlying caches. Re-querying permissions alone is insufficient for inherited or role/team-based grants.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sender check crashes when Integration metadata has no sender

The check dereferences integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] unconditionally. Integrations created through the pipeline itself only receive metadata.sender when state contains sender (build_integration), and no pipeline view binds sender into state, so pipeline-created or older orphaned ACTIVE integrations can lack metadata.sender. When such an integration exists without an OrganizationIntegration, dispatch raises KeyError/TypeError and returns a 500 instead of a graceful installation error or a successful relink.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: unconditionally accessing `integration.metadata['sender']['login']` will raise a KeyError when the `sender` key is missing from metadata.

false_positives.candidate:
Sender validation is bypassed when no Integration row exists yet

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the Integration.DoesNotExist branch immediately returns pipeline.next_step() without comparing the pipeline's github_authenticated_user to the user who installed the GitHub app. Creation of the Integration row by the GitHub webhook is asynchronous and can race or be missed, so an attacker who knows or guesses a victim's incremental GitHub installation_id and starts the linking flow before that row exists can finish the pipeline; build_integration then creates/links the integration based only on installation_id. This defeats the new mismatch protection and can attach a victim's GitHub installation to the attacker's Sentry organization.

GitHub token exchange failures can raise instead of showing the installation error

OAuthLoginView calls safe_urlopen for the OAuth access-token exchange outside the try block that only covers safe_urlread/parse_qsl, and then calls get_user_info without exception handling. If GitHub's token or user endpoints return an HTTP error, time out, or otherwise fail at the safe_urlopen layer, the exception propagates as an unhandled 500 rather than rendering the github-integration-failed page that the PR intends for bad or reused authorization codes. Both external calls need to be covered and mapped to the error response.

Integration lookups do not filter by provider

The lookups in GitHubInstallation use Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) even though Integration identity is unique only by (provider, external_id), not by external_id alone. If another integration provider has a record with the same external_id as a GitHub installation_id, get() raises MultipleObjectsReturned, which is not caught because only DoesNotExist is handled, causing a 500; it could also select the wrong integration's metadata for the sender comparison. The queries should filter provider to the GitHub provider key.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found path

The test stubs GET /app/installations/{id} to return 404, but its callback request supplies state ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, which does not match the pipeline signature. OAuthLoginView therefore returns the generic invalid-installation page before GitHubInstallation/build_integration can call get_installation_info, so the test would pass even if the 404 handling in build_integration were broken or removed. The callback should use the valid pipeline state and assert the installation-not-found outcome.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup registers removal of a literal "alias" instead of the created IdPs

In testCacheIDPForLogin the loop creates IdPs with aliases idp-alias-0..19 (and later idp-alias-20 at line 425) but registers cleanup as testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove, i.e. for an IdP literally named "alias" rather than the loop variable alias / the created alias. The created providers are therefore not removed (and removing the non-existent "alias" can itself fail during cleanup), leaving 21 extra IdPs in the shared test realm that can leak into other test methods of the class and make count-based cache assertions order-dependent and flaky.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: the test cleanup is referencing the literal string 'alias' instead of the dynamically created 'idp-alias-' + i (or the alias variable).

false_positives.candidate:
Update invalidation compares an organization-aware wrapped model against a raw model

update() obtains the original via getById(), which returns createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(): for an IdP linked to an organization its isEnabled() is overridden to also require the organization (and the organization feature) to be enabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() then evaluates getLoginPredicate() on that wrapped original but on the raw updated model, while the JPA getForLogin query that populated the cache filters on the raw enabled flag. Example: an enabled, public IdP of a disabled organization is in the cached login list (raw enabled=true), but the wrapped original reports isEnabled()=false; disabling the IdP (updated enabled=false) makes both predicates false, so no login-cache invalidation is registered and the stale internal id remains in the cached getForLogin result, violating the contract that getForLogin returns only enabled login IdPs.

Shared getLoginPredicate() semantics changed to exclude private organization brokers

LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() is a public SPI predicate previously defined purely by the LoginFilter values (enabled, not link-only, not hidden on login, matching getLoginSearchOptions()). This change additionally requires any organization-linked IdP to have kc.org.broker.public=true. That silently changes the meaning for every existing caller of the predicate, not just the new cache-invalidation code: a private organization broker that is legitimately usable once its organization is known (e.g. after organization identification) is now classified as never available for login, and the predicate no longer corresponds to the LoginFilter enum documented as containing all fields considered for login availability. The broker-public check should be local to the cache-invalidation decision instead of redefining the shared predicate.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No tests lock in that SQL expressions stay disabled

The change adds an early rejection for QueryTypeSQL and stubs out the SQL DB in pkg/expr/sql/db.go, but no test files are changed. There is therefore no regression test proving a SQL expression is rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, and no updated/skipped coverage for the existing SQL parser/command tests whose TablesList/QueryFramesInto calls now always return 'not implemented'. Add tests for the disabled behavior on both query-parsing entry points and update or explicitly skip the now-obsolete DuckDB-backed SQL tests so CI demonstrates the CVE fix rather than merely failing or silently losing coverage.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment points out that the DB methods in pkg/expr/sql/db.go are stubbed out with hardcoded 'not implemented' errors. While the candidate issue focuses on updating tests, it explicitly identifies this exact change ('stubs out the SQL DB in pkg/expr/sql/db.go' and 'TablesList/QueryFramesInto calls now always return not implemented') and points out that existing tests calling these methods will now fail because of it.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy SQL-command entry point is not explicitly disabled

UnmarshalSQLCommand still constructs a SQLCommand through NewSQLCommand without any disabled/feature check. The newer ExpressionQueryReader is explicitly described as not yet replacing the existing transform.go query path, so this legacy path remains reachable. It is currently blocked only incidentally because sql.TablesList calls the new stub DB and fails, which is then reported as a generic invalid-SQL BadRequest. If the stub DB is later implemented or replaced, this entry point would re-enable SQL execution without passing through the reader's kill-switch and could re-expose the DuckDB RCE/LFI surface. Reject SQL explicitly in UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand, or in the service pipeline builder, with the same disabled/not-implemented error used by the reader.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock

GetWebAssets releases the read lock before acquiring the write lock, but never rechecks entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring it. Every goroutine that observed a nil cache during a cold start will therefore serialize on the write lock and repeat the manifest file read and parsing, overwriting the cache each time, while the exclusive lock also blocks fast-path readers for the duration of that I/O. On a burst of concurrent index requests at startup this defeats the cache for that burst and unnecessarily serializes disk I/O; recheck the cache inside the write lock (respecting Dev mode) and return the already-loaded value when another goroutine populated it.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `GetWebAssets` fails to re-check if the cache was populated by another goroutine after releasing the read lock and acquiring the write lock (incomplete double-checked locking).

false_positives.candidate:
No concurrent regression test exercises the claimed race fix

This change adds mutex synchronization around entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines. Sequential tests would not have triggered the original data race under the race detector, so removing or misplacing one of the new lock operations in the future would not be caught. Add a same-package test that resets the global cache, serves a valid assets-manifest fixture via cfg.StaticRootPath, hammers GetWebAssets concurrently in non-Dev mode, and is run with -race.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors with full ID lists

The new cleanup paths at lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579 call r.log.Error unconditionally after successful fetches/deletes, passing a nil err and the entire ids slice (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize, e.g. 32767 IDs in the new test). Normal cleanup will therefore emit multiple huge error-level log lines per batch per annotation type, flooding logs, triggering error alerting, and masking real failures. These should be Debug-level (or removed), should not log the full ID list, and errors should only be logged where they are actually returned.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: the code is using the Error log level (`r.log.Error`) to log non-error/debugging information during normal execution, which will pollute/flood production error logs. Both suggest changing the log level to Debug.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Ticker change runs every cleanup job ten times more often

Changing the global cleanup ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute affects all jobs in clean(), not only annotation cleanup: expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, user invites, short URLs, and query history will also run ten times as often. This increases database and filesystem load and lock contention on every Grafana instance, is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix described in the PR, and is not documented or made configurable. The interval should be reverted to 10 minutes or separately justified and scoped to annotations only.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same problem: changing the cleanup job ticker interval from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which causes cleanup tasks to run ten times more frequently and leads to increased database load and contention.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteByIDs can exceed parameter limits on non-SQLite databases

For every database except the special-cased SQLite path, deleteByIDs builds a single DELETE with one placeholder per fetched ID, and the number of IDs is bounded only by the configurable AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize. PostgreSQL and MySQL prepared statements are limited to 65535 parameters, so a larger configured batch size that previously worked with the subquery DELETE will now fail on every batch and abort cleanup. The delete should be chunked into bounded groups for all dialects rather than only working around SQLite.

SQLite ID list construction is quadratic for large batches

The SQLite branch rebuilds the IN list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside the loop, copying the entire accumulated string on every iteration. For the 32767-ID batch exercised by the new test this is O(n^2) copying (gigabytes of intermediate copying) on each affected annotation type, undermining the large-batch support the branch is meant to add. Build the list with strings.Builder or strings.Join instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Storage failures are recorded in the wrong duration metric

When Storage.Create fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration; Update has the same mistake on its storage-error path, and DeleteCollection records its asynchronous legacy result with recordStorageDuration. Storage and legacy latency/error dashboards and alerts will therefore attribute failures to the wrong backend and can hide unified-storage errors.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment identifies a specific bug in DeleteCollection where a storage failure incorrectly calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration. The candidate issue points out the same type of swapped metric bug across the class, specifically mentioning Create, Update, and the opposite swap in DeleteCollection's async legacy result. Although the candidate misses the exact line in DeleteCollection's storage failure path (or confuses it with the legacy path), it clearly identifies the same underlying copy-paste bug regarding swapped recordStorageDuration and recordLegacyDuration calls.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete uses the object name as the Prometheus kind label

The successful Delete path calls recordStorageDuration with name where the other methods pass options.Kind. Prometheus labels must be bounded; using a distinct resource name for every deleted object creates unbounded metric cardinality, increasing memory and query cost and breaking comparisons by kind. It should pass options.Kind like the error path and other methods.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: passing `name` instead of `options.Kind` when recording metrics, which is inconsistent with other methods.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and can be cancelled immediately

Create derives its 10-second legacy-write context from the incoming request context; the same pattern is used for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. Once the API handler finishes and returns the response, the request context is cancelled, so an in-flight legacy write can be aborted despite the 10-second timeout. This can silently leave legacy storage without the backup write that mode 3 is intended to provide. The context needs to be detached from request cancellation while preserving request values such as authentication.

Async legacy Create races with use of the returned object

Create passes the original obj to Legacy.Create in a goroutine after Storage.Create has returned created from that same input. Storage implementations may mutate obj or return an object aliasing it, while the caller will proceed to serialize or otherwise use created. The legacy store can therefore concurrently read or mutate shared object state, causing a data race or changing the response after unified storage has completed. The object should be deep-copied before launching the asynchronous legacy write.

Update reuses objInfo instead of propagating the unified-storage result to legacy

Update passes the same UpdatedObjectInfo independently to unified storage and then asynchronously to legacy storage, dropping the previous updateWrapper behavior. UpdatedObject will be computed a second time against legacy's old object, so the two stores can receive different content when their old objects or resource versions differ, and implementations that cache or mutate the decoded object can make the second computation incorrect. Legacy should receive the same updated object that unified storage accepted, as the previous implementation ensured.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight asynchronous legacy writes

Mode 3 launches fire-and-forget goroutines for legacy writes but keeps no WaitGroup or other tracking. Destroy immediately destroys both storages, so shutdown can terminate or close legacy storage while writes are still running, losing backup writes or causing use-after-destroy failures. Asynchronous work needs to be tracked and drained before the underlying storages are destroyed.

Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes

The new tests invoke Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection but do not wait for or assert the legacy goroutines, and both stores share one testify mock with indistinguishable expectations. The tests therefore pass even if a legacy method is never called, is called with the wrong object, or fails asynchronously after the test returns. They need synchronization and separate assertions that each legacy operation eventually runs with the expected arguments.

Mode 3 playlist integration test assumes synchronous legacy visibility

The new mode 3 integration cases reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates or updates through the Kubernetes API and immediately reads the same data through the legacy playlist API. Mode 3 now writes to legacy in a background goroutine, so there is no ordering guarantee that the legacy rows exist when those immediate assertions run. This introduces intermittent integration-test failures unless the test polls for legacy visibility or the helper waits for asynchronous writes to settle.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grafana rule list items are rendered without a React key

false_positives.candidate:
Pause action is never shown in the ruler-free list view

The pause menu item requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) in addition to canPause. In the new list view rulerRule is intentionally undefined, so even though the Grafana Prometheus ability can set canPause to true, the Pause/Unpause item is never rendered there. Delete action is never shown in the ruler-free list view

The Delete menu item is gated by `canDelete && rulerRule`. In the new list view rulerRule is undefined, so the newly added Grafana Prometheus delete ability has no effect and users with delete permission cannot delete a Grafana rule from the list's More menu. The underlying delete handler in RuleActionsButtons.V2 operates on the rule identifier and does not need the ruler rule object.

skipToken does not neutralize the Duplicate ability for non-Grafana rules

useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities converts skipToken to undefined, and useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities treats an undefined rule as supported because useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable returns loading=false for no rule. Duplicate therefore becomes [AlwaysSupported, grafana AlertingRuleCreate permission]. When AlertRuleMenu renders a cloud/data-source rule, a user who has Grafana rule-create permission but not the external rule-create permission incorrectly gets the Duplicate action via the OR of ruler and Grafana abilities.

Combined-rule abilities no longer treat federated groups as immutable

useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously used isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) and marked rules in federated groups as not supported for update/delete/pause-type actions. The refactored useAllRulerRuleAbilities hardcodes isFederated to false, so federated Mimir rule groups can now appear editable/removable in consumers using CombinedRule abilities, regressing the previous protection for federated groups.

Grafana recording rules lose pause and export abilities

The Prometheus-based abilities gate Pause, Restore, DeletePermanently, and ModifyExport on prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule). The ruler-based path used isGrafanaManagedAlertRule, which includes Grafana recording rules as well as alerting rules. As a result, Grafana recording rules in the ruler-free list view cannot be paused or exported even though those actions were supported for them through the ruler-based path.

Grafana rule link drops the returnTo parameter

The deleted GrafanaRuleListItem built its view href with createReturnTo() so the rule detail view received a returnTo query parameter pointing back to the current list context. The new component links directly to /alerting/grafana/${uid}/view without returnTo, so navigation back from a rule opened from the filtered/group list loses the list context that the previous link explicitly preserved.

Menu test codifies the missing Delete item instead of covering it

The test grants AlertingRuleDelete globally and in folder access control and defines a delete menu selector, but the More-menu test expects exactly four menu items and never asserts Delete. This hides the regression that Delete is not rendered in the ruler-free Grafana list even for users with delete permission.

Interpolating before querySupportsSplitting can defeat the $__range split guard

runSplitQuery() now replaces template variables in query.expr at line 299 and only afterwards, at line 300, partitions queries with querySupportsSplitting(). That helper is documented at lines 282-288 to keep queries containing $__range, $__range_s or $__range_ms out of splitting so the backend can interpolate the range against the unsplit time range. If applyTemplateVariables() substitutes those range variables (as it does other variables such as $__auto/$step in the new test), the marker is gone before the check, the query is classified as splittable, and every time chunk is sent with the range value frozen from the original panel range, producing incorrect rate/range results instead of the intended single unsplit request. The splittability check needs to be done on the pre-interpolation expression or range variables must be provably preserved and covered by a test.

Shard-split queries are interpolated twice, once per shard group

runShardSplitQuery() interpolates every target with datasource.applyTemplateVariables() at line 52, adds the __stream_shard__ selector, and then delegates each shard group to runSplitQuery() (line 163), which after this change interpolates the same targets again at querySplitting.ts:299. The updated test codifies this: a single target now triggers applyTemplateVariables 5 times (1 initial + 1 per shard sub-request). Template interpolation with scopedVars and ad-hoc filters (request.filters is passed in both places) is not a guaranteed idempotent operation: variable values containing '$', $__auto/step derivation, and ad-hoc filter injection into the stream selector can be applied a second time to an already interpolated/shard-augmented expression, and the redundant work scales with the number of shard groups. runSplitQuery needs a way for the shard path to skip re-interpolation, or the shard path should not pre-interpolate beyond what shard grouping requires.

Empty-expression filtering now happens before interpolation in shard splitting

The filters at lines 50-51 run before the interpolation map at line 52, whereas the previous code interpolated first and then dropped queries with no expr. A target whose expr is only a template variable (e.g. expr: '$q') that expands to an empty string now passes the filter, is interpolated to '', and continues into groupTargetsByQueryType()/getSelectorForShardValues() and on to execution as an empty LogQL query instead of being ignored, causing shard-label fetching and/or a Loki parse error for a query that should have been dropped. The expr emptiness check should also (or instead) be applied to the interpolated result; the same filter-before-map pattern was introduced in runSplitQuery at querySplitting.ts:296-299.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit is enforced by a non-atomic count-then-insert and can be exceeded concurrently

CreateOrUpdateDevice runs CountDevices in one DB session and, if the count is below the limit, performs the INSERT/UPSERT in a separate session with no transaction, lock, or other serialization. Concurrent first-time requests for distinct devices (across goroutines or Grafana instances sharing the database) can all observe count == limit-1 and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. The check-and-create needs to be atomic, e.g. inside a transaction with appropriate locking.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same race condition where concurrent requests can bypass the device limit check due to a non-atomic count-then-insert operation, and both suggest using a database transaction or lock to fix it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Failed device-limit check poisons the local cache and lets the device in on retry

tagDeviceUI writes the device key to localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice and never removes it when that call fails. A new device over the limit is denied on its first request, but the cache entry remains for the 29-minute cache TTL; on its next request tagDeviceUI returns nil on the cache hit without touching the store, TagDevice returns nil, and Anonymous.Authenticate grants an identity. The configured limit is therefore bypassed after a single denied attempt on the same instance. Set the cache entry only after a successful store write, or delete it when CreateOrUpdateDevice returns an error.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `tagDeviceUI` populates `localCache` before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, meaning if the device limit is reached and an error occurs, the cache remains populated for 29 minutes and allows subsequent requests to bypass the limit.

false_positives.candidate:
Provider signature changes are not reflected in wire generation, breaking the server build

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore and constructs the store itself, and ProvideAnonDBStore now takes an int64 deviceLimit that wire cannot supply. The checked-in pkg/server/wire_gen.go is not updated in this PR and still calls both providers with their old signatures, so the server package will not compile; the wire provider set also still needs to drop/replace ProvideAnonDBStore and be regenerated.

Anonymous authentication now blocks on the database with no timeout or panic isolation

Authenticate previously tagged the device in a goroutine with a 2-minute background-context timeout and panic recovery; it now calls TagDevice synchronously with the request context and no deadline. A slow or stalled device-store query (count plus upsert, now on the auth path) blocks anonymous authentication indefinitely, a client disconnect cancels the tagging via the request context, and a panic in tagging now propagates into authentication. Keep the synchronous enforcement needed for the limit, but bound it with a timeout context and recover from panics.

updateDevice can falsely report the limit reached for an existing MySQL device

updateDevice treats RowsAffected == 0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, RowsAffected for UPDATE counts changed rows, not matched rows; when an already-known device is re-tagged (e.g. via another instance whose local cache is cold) within the same second and with unchanged client_ip/user_agent, the stored updated_at has second precision so nothing changes and MySQL reports 0. A legitimate, already-counted device is then denied as if it were new. Use a matched-row check (existence SELECT, or found-rows semantics) instead of relying on changed-row counts.

No test covers an existing device updating successfully while at the limit, or client-level denial

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a second, new device is rejected when the limit is 1. The other half of the feature branch—an already-registered device calling CreateOrUpdateDevice again while count >= limit must succeed via updateDevice—is untested, as is Anonymous.Authenticate returning an error (and no identity) on ErrDeviceLimitReached and unlimited behavior with limit 0 end to end (impl_test.go always uses a default cfg with limit 0). A regression in updateDevice would ship undetected.

New device_limit option is not added to default configuration or documentation

The PR reads [auth.anonymous] device_limit into Cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit but does not add it to conf/defaults.ini (or the configuration documentation). Operators have no discoverable way to learn the option exists or that 0 means unlimited and negative values are also treated as unlimited by the deviceLimit > 0 guard. Add the setting with its default and semantics to defaults.ini and the auth.anonymous docs.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are loaded only during web requests

I18n.translate loads only config.locale before delegating to the backend, while the new code loads the site-default and English fallback files only from ApplicationController#set_locale. Background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, console code, and model-level translations therefore query fallback locales whose YAML files were never loaded and receive 'translation missing'. Worse, argument-less lookups cache that missing result in the LRU cache at lines 71-76, so the missing string can persist after a later web request loads the fallback locale. Fallback loading belongs in the translation/load path, not only in the controller.

Every fallback lookup depends on SiteSetting and can fail outside a ready request stack

FallbackLocaleList#[] unconditionally calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, and I18n::Backend::Fallbacks invokes this method for translation misses in any context, not just after ApplicationController has already resolved the locale. If the setting is blank or the settings/DB layer is unavailable during boot, migrations, seeding, or job startup, a routine missing translation becomes a NoMethodError or database error instead of falling back to :en. The hot missing-translation path should use a guarded or cached default that safely degrades to English.

Cached translations ignore the dynamic fallback chain

The LRU cache key contains only the key, current locale, and backend object_id, but after this change the result for a key missing in the current locale also depends on SiteSetting.default_locale, which FallbackLocaleList reads dynamically. Changing the site default locale does not change the cache key or clear the cache, so users can keep receiving text in the previous fallback language until entries are evicted or translations are manually reloaded.

No tests cover the new fallback behaviour

The pull request introduces a custom FallbackLocaleList, backend Fallbacks inclusion, fallback-file loading, and a controller hook, but adds no specs. There is no coverage proving that a key missing in the user locale resolves first to the site default and then to English, that fallback locale files are loaded before lookup, or that pluralized/interpolated fallback translations work, so regressions would silently surface as 'translation missing' text.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

Plural embedded hydration replaces missing records with undefined and discards the ids

For *_ids keys the new code maps every id through _lookupSubType and unconditionally assigns the result and deletes the original key. When an id is not present in the side-loaded root collection (or the collection is absent), _lookupSubType returns undefined, so the model property becomes an array containing undefined entries and the original ids are lost. When categoryId is null the Rails controller substitutes SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id, but the save callback ignores the returned category_id and instead sets category from the stale local categoryId via Discourse.Category.findById(null). The row is then displayed with no category even though the server stored the uncategorized category, and a later edit action dereferences host.category.id (line 26), which can throw for exactly these rows. There is no uniqueness validation on host and the new table has no unique index. An admin (or a double submit) can create two EmbeddableHost rows for the same hostname with different categories; record_for_host then uses .first with no ordering, so TopicEmbed.import can assign imported topics to an arbitrary one of those categories and the result can change as rows are added or removed.

The format validation on line 2 explicitly permits host values such as example.com:8080 and the before_validation only strips scheme and path, so the port is stored. record_for_host compares lower(host) to URI(host).host, and Ruby's URI#host strips the port, so it compares 'example.com:8080' to 'example.com' and never matches. Because the resulting post uses raw_html rendering, that injected markup is stored and served without sanitization. The URL and link text must be HTML/attribute escaped, or the anchor must be built with a DOM builder.

However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed polling crashes on items without full content

poll_feed unconditionally calls i.content.scrub for every feed item. Many RSS/Atom items provide only a description or summary and no content/content:encoded element, in which case i.content is nil and this raises NoMethodError. The job is configured with retry: false and has no per-item error handling, so one such item aborts the entire hourly import and prevents all remaining items from being processed. The code should fall back to description/summary when content is absent and isolate failures per item.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: calling `i.content.scrub` when `i.content` is nil (because RSS feeds often only provide a description/summary instead of full content), which raises a nil/NoMethodError. Both also suggest falling back to `description`.

false_positives.candidate:
Raw-HTML posts bypass HTML sanitization

Post#cook returns the stored raw text verbatim for the new raw_html cook method, and TopicEmbed uses that method for imported content. The feed-polling path passes arbitrary RSS/Atom HTML directly to TopicEmbed without Readability's tag whitelist or any other sanitizer, after which the result is stored as cooked HTML and rendered raw. A malicious or compromised feed item containing script tags, event-handler attributes, or other active markup therefore becomes stored XSS for forum visitors. Imported HTML must be passed through a whitelist sanitizer before it is saved as cooked content.

Remote import performs unrestricted server-side fetching

TopicEmbed.import_remote calls open(url).read before TopicEmbed.import performs its scheme check, with no timeout, response-size limit, or restriction on redirect targets or private IP addresses. The on-demand retrieval flow validates only the initial URL's host, while open-uri follows HTTP redirects, so an embeddable-host URL can redirect the server to localhost, link-local, or internal services and have the fetched content converted into a public topic; a very large response is also read entirely into memory. Fetching needs an explicit HTTP(S) client with scheme/final-URI validation, private-address blocking, timeouts, and a size cap.

Unknown embed URLs enqueue unbounded background jobs

Every request for an unknown embed_url enqueues a RetrieveTopic job, and the loading page automatically reloads and repeats the request. The Referer check is trivially spoofable by non-browser clients, and TopicRetriever's 60-second throttle is only applied after a job is dequeued, so an attacker can flood Sidekiq with jobs and use distinct URLs on the embeddable host to trigger repeated outbound fetch attempts. Host validation and an atomic throttle/deduplication check need to happen before enqueueing, with throttled requests returning the loading response without creating another job.

Embed creation has a check-then-create race

TopicEmbed.import first queries for an existing embed and then creates the topic, post, and embed record without any locking. The scheduled feed poller and an on-demand RetrieveTopic job (or two concurrent retrieves) can both observe no embed for the same URL and both create content; the loser then hits the unique index on topic_embeds.embed_url at create! and the whole job fails with RecordNotUnique even though the URL was successfully imported by the winner. Creation should be made atomic or rescue RecordNotUnique and return the existing embed's post.

Disqus import now depends on live thread URLs and drops the category option

The importer previously created each topic locally from the Disqus export, but now calls TopicEmbed.import_remote, which fetches t[:link] over the network for every thread. If a linked article has moved, returns 404, or the import runs offline, open() raises and aborts the entire import, losing comments that are fully present in the export file. The same change removes the --category Thor option, breaking existing import invocations that pass it and leaving no way to place imported threads in a category. The export-based creation needs to remain as a fallback and the category option needs to be plumbed through to topic creation.

Only root-relative URLs are absolutized in imported content

absolutize_urls only rewrites href/src values that start with '/'. Relative references such as 'images/photo.jpg' or 'page2.html', which are common in feed content, are left unchanged and will resolve against the Discourse host instead of the source article, producing broken images and links. Conversely, a protocol-relative URL like '//cdn.example.com/x.js' starts with '/' and is incorrectly rewritten onto the article's host. All non-absolute references should be resolved with URI.join against the source URL, which handles relative, root-relative, and protocol-relative forms correctly.

Feed-setting guard specs pass without exercising the guards

The specs for 'requires feed_polling_url' and 'requires embed_by_username' stub only the setting named in the example. Jobs::PollFeed#execute checks feed_polling_enabled? first, and that setting defaults to false, so execute short-circuits before the stubbed setting is ever consulted and poll_feed is never called regardless of whether the URL/username guards exist. These examples would still pass if those two guards were deleted. Each example needs the preceding conditions stubbed to their enabling values (enabled true, and a present URL for the username example) so only the guard under test can block polling.

Slots inside a date override bypass the busy-time check

In checkIfIsAvailable, when a slot's date matches a date override and the slot is inside the override window, the function returns true immediately. It never reaches the busy.every(...) check against existing Cal bookings and connected-calendar busy times. A fixed or round-robin host who has a date override on a day can therefore be shown as available at times when they already have a booking or calendar event, allowing double-bookings on override days.

Only the first same-day date override is considered

The dateOverrides.find(...) callback returns true as soon as the slot falls outside the first override that shares the slot's date. If a user has two override ranges on the same day (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-17:00, which Cal.com allows as separate availability rows), a slot inside the second range is judged against the first range, find() stops, and checkIfIsAvailable returns false. Valid slots in the second and later override ranges of the day are incorrectly removed, notably for fixed hosts in round-robin events.

Override containment check admits partially overlapping slots

A slot is treated as inside a date override unless its end is at/before the override start or its start is strictly after the override end. A slot that starts before the override begins but ends inside it (e.g. 13:30-14:30 for a 14:00-18:00 override) is not flagged as outside and is reported available, and a slot starting exactly at the override end is also treated as inside because isAfter is used instead of isSameOrAfter. Bookings can therefore start before the host's override availability begins or exactly when it ends.

Working-hours gate is wrong for split schedules and days off

The workingHours.find(...) check returns 'outside working hours' if ANY working-hour entry for that weekday does not cover the slot, so a host with split hours (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00 on the same day) has afternoon slots rejected because the morning entry does not cover them. Conversely, if no entry lists the slot's weekday at all, find() returns nothing and the check passes entirely, so a fixed host can still be booked on a day off whenever a round-robin host's availability generated that slot. Both cases defeat the fixed-host enforcement this block was added for.

The new code converts the override wall time by the invitee-minus-organizer offset and keeps only hour/minute, discarding the resulting date, while the activeOverrides filter above still selects overrides by comparing the unshifted UTC-encoded start against the invitee day. For an organizer ahead of the invitee (e.g. a 09:00 override in UTC+10 viewed from UTC), the converted time is 23:00 on the previous invitee day, but the filter attaches it to the following invitee day, so the slot is offered a day late instead of on the correct day.

The PR description states the main fix is that date overrides of fixed hosts restrict round-robin events, but the only added test re-queries a personal (non-team) event in Asia/Dhaka versus Asia/Kolkata and expects identical UTC slots. This can break server startup/token issuance for deployments with custom grants. Provide a default method (for example returning the unknown shortcut) instead of an abstract method, or otherwise handle factories that do not supply a shortcut.

OAuth2GrantType.Context copy constructor was removed

The public Context(Context) copy constructor was removed while Context is the object passed to custom OAuth2GrantType implementations. Since TokenManager.initToken now calls this for every access token, previously working flows/custom grants whose grant string is not identical to a registered OAuth2GrantType factory id will fail token creation with a server error instead of issuing a token. New order() method is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is an SPI loaded through ServiceLoader, but order() was added as an abstract method. Existing external or test implementations compiled against the previous interface do not implement it, so recompilation fails and already-compiled providers will throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration sorting invokes order(). This can prevent crypto-provider detection at startup. order() should be a default method, with only providers that need non-default precedence overriding it.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding abstract order() to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations that do not define it. The candidate provides additional consequences and a default-method fix consistent with the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Equal-priority crypto providers are silently selected in classpath-dependent order

The change removes the previous fail-fast error for multiple CryptoProvider implementations and instead sorts by order() and silently uses the first provider, logging the others only at debug level. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so when more than one is present the winner depends on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order. In particular, an environment accidentally containing both FIPS and non-FIPS providers could silently run with the non-FIPS provider instead of failing, creating a compliance and security risk. The providers need distinct priorities, especially for FIPS, or detection should fail/warn prominently on a tie for the highest priority.

ES384 and ES512 tests reuse a default P-256 key and only test self round-tripping

The test constructor generates one EC key pair without specifying a curve, normally P-256, and reuses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512. Consequently the 48-byte ES384 and especially 66-byte ES512 integer paths and DER long-form sequence lengths over 127 bytes produced by real P-521 signatures are not exercised. The assertions also only check that this provider can decode its own encoding; they never verify the generated ASN.1 DER against the original JDK signature or with JDK Signature.verify(). Mutually inverse encoding/decoding errors could therefore pass while producing non-interoperable signatures. Tests should generate P-256, P-384, and P-521 keys respectively and verify interoperability with the JDK signature implementation.

No test covers ServiceLoader registration or the new provider-ordering selection

The central behavior of this change is that AuthzClientCryptoProvider is discoverable through META-INF/services and that CryptoIntegration chooses the highest-order provider when several providers are present, but the only new test directly constructs AuthzClientCryptoProvider. A broken service registration, an incorrect order value, or a regression in CryptoIntegration sorting would not be caught. A test should load providers through CryptoIntegration/ServiceLoader and assert that the authz provider is selected when alone and that a higher-order provider such as DefaultCryptoProvider wins when both are present.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() can leave most flusher processes running after the timeout expires

join() computes the deadline before calling self.next_step.join(timeout), which may consume the entire timeout, and then breaks out of the process loop when no time remains. terminate() is only reached for processes the loop has already visited, so remaining spawn processes are neither terminated nor joined. Because strategies are closed/joined and recreated in the same parent process during rebalancing, leftover daemon flushers can keep polling their shards alongside the replacement SpanFlusher and race it to produce segments. All processes should be signalled to stop/terminate before waiting on each of them subject to the deadline.

A value of 0 is silently treated as unspecified because of `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, while a negative value makes num_processes negative and produces an empty process_to_shards_map. With no workers, submit() has no buffers or backpressure state to check but still forwards messages to the committer, so spans can be committed and accumulate in Redis without ever being flushed. Fail fast on flusher_processes < 1 (and on an empty assigned-shard set) instead of starting a consumer with no flusher.

Unhealthy flusher is replaced before the old worker has actually stopped

_ensure_processes_alive() only signals a spawn process with kill() and never waits for it to exit; for threading.Thread workers the isinstance check skips termination entirely. It then immediately starts a replacement and overwrites self.processes/self.buffers for the same shards, losing the handle to the old worker. The old and new workers can therefore both run SpanFlusher.main() over the same shards, concurrently calling flush_segments/produce/done_flush_segments and potentially producing duplicate segments. The old worker should be terminated and joined (and the thread-based test path handled explicitly) before its replacement is started.

Multiprocess flusher test checks counts but not shard routing or delivery

test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts that there are two processes and that the shard lists total four entries. A broken mapping with duplicated and missing shards (for example [[0, 0], [1, 2]]) would still pass, and the test never submits spans or asserts that segments from each assigned shard are produced. false_positives.candidate:
Queues are unbounded, so the strategy provides no backpressure

FixedQueuePool creates each queue.Queue with no maxsize and submit() always returns after put(). Because SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit therefore never blocks or rejects a message, Arroyo can keep polling Kafka and accumulating decoded WorkItems, OffsetTracker entries, and queued payloads in memory whenever workers fall behind—the exact slow-consumer scenario this mode is meant to handle. This contradicts the strategy docstring's claimed natural backpressure and can OOM the consumer instead of pausing consumption.

Failed work items are marked complete and become committable

OrderedQueueWorker catches every exception from result_processor, then its finally block calls offset_tracker.complete_offset(). SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit has the same problem for grouping/submission failures at lines 317-325: it logs, adds the offset, and immediately completes it. A failed uptime result can consequently be committed as if successfully processed, with no retry or DLQ handling, despite the class docstring promising that offsets are committed only after successful processing.

Closing one strategy shuts down the factory-shared queue pool

ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and passes that same pool to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy it creates. Arroyo closes the old strategy when partitions are revoked and then asks the same factory for a new strategy, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), shutting down all queues and workers. The replacement strategy then reuses a dead pool; subsequent queue.put calls raise queue.ShutDown, which submit() catches and marks complete, so messages after a rebalance can be silently dropped and committed.

Graceful shutdown does not drain queued work

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True before calling Queue.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker checks that flag in its while condition, so after finishing—or waking from—its current item it exits even if its queue still contains items that immediate=False was supposed to let it drain. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() also never waits for the queues to empty before shutting the pool down, so close() abandons queued work rather than completing it before Arroyo tears down the assignment.

terminate() can commit offsets after the strategy has terminated

terminate() sets shutdown_event but does not join commit_thread, unlike close(). _commit_loop waits for one second and then computes and calls commit_function without rechecking shutdown_event before committing, so a terminated strategy whose partitions may already have been revoked can still invoke Arroyo's commit callback after termination.

Group assignment uses Python's randomized hash()

get_queue_for_group() uses built-in hash(group_key), whose result for strings is randomized per Python process unless PYTHONHASHSEED is fixed. The mapping is therefore not the consistent hashing claimed in the docstring across restarts or across consumer processes; the same subscription can move to a different worker/queue in another process, weakening the within-group ordering guarantee for results that are not confined to one process/partition assignment. A stable digest-based hash should be used instead.

Commit scan is O(backlog) every second and holds the partition lock

get_committable_offsets() runs every second and iterates range(start, max_offset + 1) while holding the partition lock. When one early offset is stuck, mark_committed never prunes all_offsets/outstanding, so every later offset for that partition makes the retained sets and the scanned range larger; the commit thread repeatedly rescans the whole backlog while blocking worker threads that need the same lock in add_offset()/complete_offset(). This degrades precisely under a slow-item backlog.

New sorted-set operations are incompatible with existing Redis segment keys

Existing span-buf:s:* keys created before this change are Redis sets, but process_spans now issues ZADD against them and the Lua script and _load_segment_data use ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN. Redis will return WRONGTYPE for those keys, so batches for traces active during deployment can fail until the keys expire after redis_ttl (3600s), and mixed old/new consumers during rollout will break each other. No key-version bump, conversion, or fallback is provided.

ZUNIONSTORE sums duplicate span scores instead of preserving timestamps

Both merge sites call ZUNIONSTORE without an AGGREGATE clause, so Redis defaults to SUM. When the same payload exists in both the destination and source sorted sets (e.g. duplicate delivery or a span stored under two keys before redirects converge), its score becomes roughly twice its end_timestamp_precise. That corrupts the ordering later used by ZPOPMIN eviction, causing duplicated spans to be retained while unrelated spans are evicted. The merge should use AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN) to preserve a real timestamp.

Insert-time eviction silently flushes incomplete segments as if complete

When a segment exceeds a hard-coded 1000 spans, ZPOPMIN discards the lowest end_timestamp_precise spans with no metric, log, or marker on the flushed segment. Those spans are permanently lost, yet flush_segments will emit the remainder as a normal segment (and the has-root flag/queue timeout may already have been set, so it flushes on the short root timeout). This replaces the previous explicit too-large-segment handling with silent partial data, ignores the configurable SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (default 1001), and with tied scores eviction order is lexicographic by payload, so even a needed span can be dropped arbitrarily.

Redirect chain resolution regresses from 10000 to 1000 hops

The loop that follows span-buf:sr redirects was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations, removing the comment that explained the 10k limit. Segment trees whose parent chain needs more than 1000 redirect hops will stop at an intermediate span ID, so later spans are merged into the wrong set and the trace is flushed as multiple split segments instead of one segment. No test or justification covers chains between 1000 and 10000 hops.

A single older or malformed message missing that field raises KeyError, aborting process_batch for every span in the batch and causing the same batch to be retried instead of only the bad message being dropped or defaulted.

The added/updated tests only supply end_timestamp_precise for existing small-segment scenarios. Nothing inserts more than 1000 spans into one segment to verify how many and which spans survive ZPOPMIN, whether the root span is retained, or how duplicate payloads merged by ZUNIONSTORE keep their scores, and there are no tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator against a datetime-ordered queryset or for negative cursors. The riskiest new behaviors in this change are therefore unverified.

Any stored error row whose sample_weight is null or 0 (for example events ingested before client sampling was enabled/configured for an allowlisted project, or events without a client_sample_rate) contributes 0 instead of 1, so historical or unsampled buckets in the retention window can drop to zero or be undercounted after the transformation. The added tests only cover events explicitly given client_sample_rate through the new factory helper.

upsampled_count is exposed as a public Discover function

The new SnQLFunction does not set private=True, unlike internal-only aggregates, so it becomes user-callable through the Discover query builder. A caller can submit upsampled_count() directly as a yAxis/field for projects and datasets that never passed the organization-events-stats allowlist and dataset checks, bypassing the gating in error_upsampling.py and receiving raw sum(sample_weight) results (including misleading zero values for transaction data).

This new file adds 'Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a' as a submodule named sentry-repo at the repository root. It is unrelated to the upsampling feature and will change checkout/CI behavior for every developer by introducing a nested Sentry checkout; it should be removed before merging.
