false_positives.candidate:
Federated recovery codes are never marked as used

After a successful validation, this code only checks whether the retrieved credential reports allCodesUsed(); it does not persist that the just-used code is now consumed. For a locally stored credential the local credential provider performs that consumption during isValid(), but for a federated user validation is delegated to the user-storage validator and that local side effect does not happen. The storage implementation added in this PR likewise only checks for a matching raw code and its getCredentials() recreates every code as unused. Consequently the same federated recovery code can be replayed indefinitely, getNextRecoveryAuthnCode() keeps prompting for the first code, and the exhaustion check/regeneration required action at lines 85-92 never triggers.

Federated recovery credential cannot be disabled or deleted

This PR adds recovery codes to supportsCredentialType(), updateCredential(), isConfiguredFor() and isValid(), but disableCredentialType() still only handles OTP types and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream() still only returns OTP. Federated credential removal (used by admin/account deletion and by RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator when all codes are used via removeStoredCredentialById) is delegated to disableCredentialType(), so a federated recovery credential silently survives deletion attempts and remains valid afterwards.

No test covers the fallback to local storage for federated users

The new test only covers a federated provider that supports recovery codes, asserting the codes land in user storage and not in the DB. The other half of the feature title/branch in CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential() - updateCredential() returning false (federated provider does not support the type, read-only storage, or imported user) and the credential then being created in the local DB and still usable for login - is never exercised for a federated user, so a regression in the local fallback for federated users would not be caught.

New exit-code contract for rolling updates is not asserted

The PR changes the recreate exit code from 4 to 3 and introduces exit code 4 for a disabled rolling-updates feature, and the documentation states that scripts should rely on the check command's exit code. However, testFeatureNotEnabled only asserts the error message for the metadata subcommand and does not assert exit code 4, no test covers the disabled-feature branch of the check subcommand, and testWrongVersions asserts only messages without asserting the new recreate exit code 3. A regression that swaps or breaks these exit codes would therefore pass the tests while breaking automation and consumers that distinguish rolling, recreate, and feature-disabled outcomes.

Existing FGAP V2 realms never receive the new Clients resource type

init() returns immediately when the realm already has an admin-permissions client, so realms that enabled FGAP V2 while the schema contained only Users will never get the new 'configure', 'map-roles-client-scope' and 'map-roles-composite' scopes nor the 'Clients' all-resource created later in this method. For those realms, creating Clients permissions fails with missing-scope errors and evaluation has no all-clients resource to fall back to. Initialization needs to be idempotent and add missing scopes/resources for existing clients, or a migration must create them.

canExchangeTo predicate now throws instead of returning a decision

canExchangeTo is a boolean authorization predicate; before this change MgmtPermissionsV2 inherited the V1 ClientPermissions implementation and callers received true/false. Now that MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() returns ClientPermissionsV2, every token-exchange permission check in a V2 deployment hits this unconditional UnsupportedOperationException, surfacing as a server error instead of a permit/deny decision and breaking client token exchange even for realms not using the new Clients permissions. The predicate should deny gracefully (or evaluate the applicable check) rather than throw.

getResourceName has no Clients branch

getResourceName only special-cases the Users resource type (returning 'All users' or the username) and falls through to resource.getDisplayName() for everything else. Client resources are created by getOrCreateResource with the client UUID as the resource name and no clientId-based display name, so permission and resource representations for the new Clients type expose a UUID, and the all-clients resource exposes 'Clients', instead of the clientId and an 'All clients' label analogous to Users. This makes the admin permission listings for clients misleading and inconsistent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
VIEW permission incorrectly grants global group manage permission

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() evaluates hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE), so an FGAP admin granted only the Groups 'view' scope passes the no-arg manage check. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup relies on auth.groups().requireManage(), therefore a view-only admin can create top-level groups and perform other operations gated only by canManage(), a privilege escalation beyond read-only access. canManage() should only accept MANAGE.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() calls hasPermission with both VIEW and MANAGE. As a result, a view-only admin passes the manage check, and canManage() should accept only MANAGE.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs

In GroupPermissionsV2, per-group authorization resources are named with the GroupModel id (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId() as the resource name), while Resource.getId() is the authorization-store UUID. This code passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission(), which looks the value up with resourceStore.findByName(), and then adds groupResource.getId() to the returned set. Callers such as UsersResource.getUsersCount() and searchForUser() pass that set to user queries as actual group ids, so members of groups the admin may view/manage are miscounted or filtered out, and the specific-group check silently falls back to the all-Groups resource. It should pass and return groupResource.getName().
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. getGroupIdsWithViewPermission passes and returns groupResource.getId() where it should use group ids (resource names). Both note that hasPermission looks resources up by name, that callers use the returned set as group filters in counts and searches, and that the check falls back to the all-groups resource.

false_positives.candidate:
Lazily created resources are not assigned their resource type

getOrCreateResource() creates a resource for a known resourceType but never calls resource.setType(resourceType), unlike AdminPermissionsSchema.init() and the V1 permission initializers which explicitly set the type. The new GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() enumerates candidates with resourceStore.findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE), so lazily created per-group resources will not be found by that lookup even after fixing which identifier is returned. The created resource should have its type set to the requested resourceType.

Existing admin-permissions clients never receive the new Groups type, scopes, or aggregate resource

AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() already exists. Realms that enabled FGAP V2 before this change therefore keep a client/resource server created from the old schema: the 'Groups' aggregate resource and group-specific scopes such as manage-members, view-members, and manage-membership are never added. On those realms group permission creation can fail when resolving scopes and GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission() can dereference a missing Groups type resource, so the new Groups support only works for newly initialized realms unless an upgrade path populates the missing scopes/resources.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore provider instead of a BouncyCastle provider

This method returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is normally a JDK provider such as Sun and can change with the JVM default keystore configuration. That violates the CryptoProvider contract that this method returns the BouncyCastle or BouncyCastle-FIPS provider. Callers using the returned provider for BouncyCastle-specific algorithms, curves, paddings, or keystore types can fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException/NoSuchProviderException or silently use a different implementation than expected. It should return null or an explicit unsupported result, consistent with having no BouncyCastle provider, rather than misidentifying an arbitrary JDK provider.
true_positives.reasoning: Both say getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider instead of the BouncyCastle provider. Same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New order() method is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is an SPI loaded through ServiceLoader, but order() was added as an abstract method. Existing external or test implementations compiled against the previous interface do not implement it, so recompilation fails and already-compiled providers will throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration sorting invokes order(). This can prevent crypto-provider detection at startup. order() should be a default method, with only providers that need non-default precedence overriding it.
true_positives.reasoning: Both say the abstract order() method added to CryptoProvider breaks backward compatibility with existing implementations. The candidate adds detail (AbstractMethodError, suggesting a default method), but the core issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Equal-priority crypto providers are silently selected in classpath-dependent order

The change removes the previous fail-fast error for multiple CryptoProvider implementations and instead sorts by order() and silently uses the first provider, logging the others only at debug level. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so when more than one is present the winner depends on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order. In particular, an environment accidentally containing both FIPS and non-FIPS providers could silently run with the non-FIPS provider instead of failing, creating a compliance and security risk. The providers need distinct priorities, especially for FIPS, or detection should fail/warn prominently on a tie for the highest priority.

ES384 and ES512 tests reuse a default P-256 key and only test self round-tripping

The test constructor generates one EC key pair without specifying a curve, normally P-256, and reuses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512. Consequently the 48-byte ES384 and especially 66-byte ES512 integer paths and DER long-form sequence lengths over 127 bytes produced by real P-521 signatures are not exercised. The assertions also only check that this provider can decode its own encoding; they never verify the generated ASN.1 DER against the original JDK signature or with JDK Signature.verify(). Mutually inverse encoding/decoding errors could therefore pass while producing non-interoperable signatures. Tests should generate P-256, P-384, and P-521 keys respectively and verify interoperability with the JDK signature implementation.

No test covers ServiceLoader registration or the new provider-ordering selection

The central behavior of this change is that AuthzClientCryptoProvider is discoverable through META-INF/services and that CryptoIntegration chooses the highest-order provider when several providers are present, but the only new test directly constructs AuthzClientCryptoProvider. A broken service registration, an incorrect order value, or a regression in CryptoIntegration sorting would not be caught. A test should load providers through CryptoIntegration/ServiceLoader and assert that the authz provider is selected when alone and that a higher-order provider such as DefaultCryptoProvider wins when both are present.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.

When the delegate group no longer exists, this returns null, whereas the persistent GroupModel implementations return a numeric count (0 when there are no subgroups). The null is propagated by GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount into GroupRepresentation.subGroupCount, so API consumers expecting a number receive no count and any caller that unboxes getSubGroupsCount() will still throw NullPointerException, only later. Returning 0L for a deleted group preserves the method contract and the representation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say getSubGroupsCount returns null, which breaks the contract that it returns a non-null count. Both also say this can cause NPEs in callers that expect a number. The candidate makes the same point.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, making the concurrency test racy and leaky

The reader thread started at line 139 is never joined and there is no latch guaranteeing it has performed a read before deletions begin. The main thread sets deletedAll at line 155 and immediately asserts at line 157 while a read may still be in flight, so a late exception can be missed; conversely the thread may not have run at all before deletion finishes, giving false confidence. The unjoined non-daemon thread can also outlive the test and keep calling managedRealm.admin() during realm cleanup or subsequent tests, causing interference and flakiness. The test should signal that reading has started and join the thread before asserting.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem. The reader thread is never joined, and the test sets deletedAll then asserts immediately, so it can miss late exceptions and become flaky. The candidate adds further detail, but its core point matches the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Same concurrent-delete NPE remains in getSubGroupsStream overloads

The fix handles modelSupplier.get() returning null in getSubGroupsCount when a cached group is deleted before its database delegate is loaded, but the three getSubGroupsStream overloads at lines 256, 262 and 268 still dereference modelSupplier.get() unconditionally. The same cache-hit/delegate-miss race therefore still throws NullPointerException and produces a server error when subgroups of a concurrently deleted group are listed or searched. These overloads should return an empty stream, or otherwise handle a null delegate consistently.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to non-existent no-argument isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()

UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method added to its superclass UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user). There is no no-argument overload in UsernamePasswordForm or AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator, so this code does not compile and blocks building the services module and running any of the added tests.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same issue: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() without the required UserModel argument.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Conditional passkeys now disabled for unidentified users, breaking initial discoverable login

isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel) requires user != null, and it is used in authenticate() and in challenge(context, error, field). Previously conditional WebAuthn data was filled when no user had been identified, which is the normal first-login case for discoverable passkeys: the credential itself supplies the user. With the new predicate, opening the username/password page initially (context.getUser() == null) never calls webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(), so no challenge/RP data or conditional-UI form is rendered and automatic passkey login cannot happen; the same loss occurs after an invalid-username challenge where the user is null. The predicate should enable passkeys based on the realm/feature setting regardless of whether a user is already identified, while only restricting the listed authenticators for an identified user.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem. isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, so authenticate() skips fillContextForm on the initial login page where no user is set yet. That breaks conditional or discoverable passkey login for unidentified users.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Comma-joined shard list corrupts flusher metric tags

When one worker handles multiple shards (including the CLI default of one flusher process), shard_tag is a value such as '0,1,2'. Passing that as a single statsd-style tag value means the commas are interpreted as tag separators, yielding shard=0 plus stray tags '1' and '2' and losing correct per-shard attribution; the wait_produce timer also inconsistently uses the key 'shards' instead of 'shard'. Emit metrics per shard or use a sanitized, single-valued tag consistently.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate's main focus is comma-joined tag values, but it also explicitly says the wait_produce timer uses the key 'shards' instead of 'shard'. That is the same inconsistency the golden comment describes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() can leave most flusher processes running after the timeout expires

join() computes the deadline before calling self.next_step.join(timeout), which may consume the entire timeout, and then breaks out of the process loop when no time remains. terminate() is only reached for processes the loop has already visited, so remaining spawn processes are neither terminated nor joined. Because strategies are closed/joined and recreated in the same parent process during rebalancing, leftover daemon flushers can keep polling their shards alongside the replacement SpanFlusher and race it to produce segments. All processes should be signalled to stop/terminate before waiting on each of them subject to the deadline.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. Breaking out of the loop once the deadline elapses skips termination of the remaining flusher processes, leaving them running.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-positive flusher process count can silently disable flushing

The new --flusher-processes option accepts any integer. A value of 0 is silently treated as unspecified because of `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, while a negative value makes num_processes negative and produces an empty process_to_shards_map. With no workers, submit() has no buffers or backpressure state to check but still forwards messages to the committer, so spans can be committed and accumulate in Redis without ever being flushed. Fail fast on flusher_processes < 1 (and on an empty assigned-shard set) instead of starting a consumer with no flusher.

Unhealthy flusher is replaced before the old worker has actually stopped

_ensure_processes_alive() only signals a spawn process with kill() and never waits for it to exit; for threading.Thread workers the isinstance check skips termination entirely. It then immediately starts a replacement and overwrites self.processes/self.buffers for the same shards, losing the handle to the old worker. The old and new workers can therefore both run SpanFlusher.main() over the same shards, concurrently calling flush_segments/produce/done_flush_segments and potentially producing duplicate segments. The old worker should be terminated and joined (and the thread-based test path handled explicitly) before its replacement is started.

Multiprocess flusher test checks counts but not shard routing or delivery

test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts that there are two processes and that the shard lists total four entries. A broken mapping with duplicated and missing shards (for example [[0, 0], [1, 2]]) would still pass, and the test never submits spans or asserts that segments from each assigned shard are produced. The core new behavior (exact shard assignment, multi-worker flushing, and aggregation across workers) is therefore untested; add an end-to-end multi-partition case asserting the exact shard set and the produced segment payloads.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Table widget feature flag renders an empty table instead of the query results

When the organization has the use-table-widget-visualization feature, tableResultComponent renders TableWidgetVisualization with columns={[]} and a hard-coded tableData containing data: [] and empty meta fields/units. It discards result.data, result.meta, fields, field aliases, custom renderers, loading state, and titles from the actual widget query. Enabling the flag therefore makes every dashboard table widget appear empty rather than showing its queried data.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: when the feature flag is enabled, TableWidgetVisualization receives hardcoded empty data and columns, so it always renders an empty table instead of the actual query results.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Browser reports with neither age nor timestamp pass validation

BrowserReportSerializer marks both age and timestamp required=False and only adds field-level validators that reject the fields when both are present. A report containing neither field therefore passes validation even though the Working Draft format requires age and the Editor's Draft format requires timestamp. The endpoint accepts and counts spec-invalid reports. Add object-level validation requiring exactly one of age or timestamp (also note the current get() checks treat a present value of 0 as absent).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate's main issue is that a report with neither field passes validation. It also explicitly notes, as a parenthetical, that the get() checks treat a present value of 0 as absent. That note matches the golden issue, though only as a secondary point.

false_positives.candidate:
Error events and replay segment events are compared using different timestamp units

fetch_error_details stores ErrorEvent.timestamp from the nodestore event timestamp, which is seconds since the epoch, while replay recording segment events use rrweb millisecond epoch timestamps. gen_request_data sorts and interleaves them with a direct '<' comparison at line 154, so an error timestamp around 1.7e9 is always considered earlier than segment timestamps around 1.7e12. All errors are consequently emitted before the first breadcrumb instead of in chronological order, and the log text also mixes second-based error times with millisecond-based breadcrumb times for Seer. Normalize one side (for example multiply the error timestamp by 1000) before sorting, merging, and formatting.

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES are only hidden while a search query is active

sortedAndFilteredAttributes returns the full sorted attribute list unchanged when searchQuery is empty; the HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES exclusion for is_segment, project_id, and received is only applied inside the search-filter branch. As a result these internal attributes are still shown in the default span Attributes view and only disappear after the user starts typing a search, which defeats the purpose of the hidden list. Apply the hidden-attribute filter before/independently of the text search filter.

Truncated issue titles exceed ISSUE_TITLE_MAX_LENGTH

_truncate_title is governed by ISSUE_TITLE_MAX_LENGTH = 50, but for an over-long title it returns title[:50].rstrip() + '...', producing up to 53 characters. The rendered PR/MR comment therefore violates the stated 50-character title limit. Truncate to max_length - len('...') before appending the ellipsis if the constant is meant to bound the final title length.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).

Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative offsets do not work on Django querysets

When enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset is negative, this code executes queryset[negative_offset:stop]. Django querysets explicitly reject negative slicing with AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'); they do not automatically handle it as the comments claim. A crafted cursor such as '0:-5:0' therefore produces an unhandled 500 rather than the claimed efficient reverse pagination. Negative offsets should be rejected with BadPaginationError or normalized before slicing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: the paginator uses negative slice offsets on Django querysets, which Django rejects with an AssertionError. The candidate points to the same code path in the optimized paginator's advanced features branch.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
organization_context.member may be None

This line unconditionally dereferences organization_context.member.has_global_access for every non-superuser request, and it is evaluated even when optimized_pagination is not requested. RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is optional and can be None for principals granted organization access without an organization membership. For such requests this newly added code raises AttributeError and breaks the previously working default pagination path; it needs a None check or an access-based check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: organization_context.member can be None for principals without a membership, such as API keys or tokens, and accessing .has_global_access then raises AttributeError. The candidate's claim about when the crash occurs differs slightly (it says even outside optimized_pagination), but the core issue is identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes on datetime sort keys

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key() applies math.floor()/math.ceil() directly to getattr(item, self.key). Its only caller, OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint, orders by -datetime, so the value is a datetime and math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError. build_cursor() calls this key function for non-empty result sets, so the first non-empty optimized audit-log page returns a 500 instead of results. It should reuse DateTimePaginator's timestamp conversion rather than the numeric Paginator implementation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: get_item_key calls math.floor/ceil on the key, but the audit logs endpoint orders by -datetime, so the value is a datetime and the call raises TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator does not convert cursor timestamps to datetimes

value_from_cursor() returns cursor.value unchanged. For audit logs that value is the millisecond epoch timestamp produced by DateTimePaginator-style cursors, but BasePaginator.build_queryset() compares it directly against the datetime column. Unlike DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor(), which converts the timestamp to an aware datetime, this passes a number into a datetime comparison, causing a database/type error or incorrect filtering on every page after the first.

BasePaginator still allows negative offsets for previous-page cursors

The new boundary handling clamps negative offsets only when cursor.is_prev is false: 'max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset'. A user-supplied cursor with is_prev=1 and a negative offset, for example '<value>:-5:1', still reaches queryset[negative:stop] and raises Django's negative-indexing AssertionError. This affects all existing BasePaginator/DateTimePaginator endpoints, not just the optimized audit-log path; negative offsets should be consistently rejected or clamped before slicing.

No tests cover OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new endpoint branch

The PR adds a new paginator class, negative-offset behavior, and a query-parameter/superuser gated branch in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint, but adds no tests. Tests using the audit-log endpoint's actual -datetime ordering, multi-page cursors, previous-page cursors, and negative offsets would have caught the datetime-key crash, timestamp-conversion bug, and Django negative-slicing failure before merge.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key are no longer serialized

BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu while creating and populating the index; it only locks for the final cache assignment. Because GetIndex returns nil until that assignment, two concurrent getOrCreateIndex/Search calls for the same NamespacedResource can both build an index. For file-backed indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory, so one can fail or contend on the on-disk index; for memory indexes both build fully and the later assignment overwrites and leaks the earlier unclosed index. Add per-key synchronization/singleflight or a double-checked cache lookup so only one build per key runs while different keys still build in parallel.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug as the golden comment. The cacheMu lock now covers only the final assignment, so concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can each build the index.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without RLock while BuildIndex now inserts into that map under a short Lock at the end of a build. Concurrent index creation (for example from the search watch goroutine handling a new namespace while init logs TotalDocs, or later lazy builds) can therefore race with this iteration, which the race detector flags and Go can turn into a fatal concurrent-map-iteration/write panic. Hold cacheMu.RLock for the iteration.

Concurrent workers therefore data-race, and a failing build's error can be overwritten by a concurrent successful build before the failing closure returns it, letting startup proceed with a missing index and producing incorrect span counts. The caller receives no server handle with which to clean up, so the opened backend and the search watch/poller (which uses context.Background) can keep running and repeated construction attempts can accumulate pollers. false_positives.candidate:
Queues are unbounded, so the strategy provides no backpressure

FixedQueuePool creates each queue.Queue with no maxsize and submit() always returns after put(). Because SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit therefore never blocks or rejects a message, Arroyo can keep polling Kafka and accumulating decoded WorkItems, OffsetTracker entries, and queued payloads in memory whenever workers fall behind—the exact slow-consumer scenario this mode is meant to handle. This contradicts the strategy docstring's claimed natural backpressure and can OOM the consumer instead of pausing consumption.

Failed work items are marked complete and become committable

OrderedQueueWorker catches every exception from result_processor, then its finally block calls offset_tracker.complete_offset(). SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit has the same problem for grouping/submission failures at lines 317-325: it logs, adds the offset, and immediately completes it. A failed uptime result can consequently be committed as if successfully processed, with no retry or DLQ handling, despite the class docstring promising that offsets are committed only after successful processing.

Closing one strategy shuts down the factory-shared queue pool

ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and passes that same pool to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy it creates. Arroyo closes the old strategy when partitions are revoked and then asks the same factory for a new strategy, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), shutting down all queues and workers. The replacement strategy then reuses a dead pool; subsequent queue.put calls raise queue.ShutDown, which submit() catches and marks complete, so messages after a rebalance can be silently dropped and committed.

Graceful shutdown does not drain queued work

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True before calling Queue.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker checks that flag in its while condition, so after finishing—or waking from—its current item it exits even if its queue still contains items that immediate=False was supposed to let it drain. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() also never waits for the queues to empty before shutting the pool down, so close() abandons queued work rather than completing it before Arroyo tears down the assignment.

terminate() can commit offsets after the strategy has terminated

terminate() sets shutdown_event but does not join commit_thread, unlike close(). _commit_loop waits for one second and then computes and calls commit_function without rechecking shutdown_event before committing, so a terminated strategy whose partitions may already have been revoked can still invoke Arroyo's commit callback after termination.

Group assignment uses Python's randomized hash()

get_queue_for_group() uses built-in hash(group_key), whose result for strings is randomized per Python process unless PYTHONHASHSEED is fixed. The mapping is therefore not the consistent hashing claimed in the docstring across restarts or across consumer processes; the same subscription can move to a different worker/queue in another process, weakening the within-group ordering guarantee for results that are not confined to one process/partition assignment. A stable digest-based hash should be used instead.

Commit scan is O(backlog) every second and holds the partition lock

get_committable_offsets() runs every second and iterates range(start, max_offset + 1) while holding the partition lock. When one early offset is stuck, mark_committed never prunes all_offsets/outstanding, so every later offset for that partition makes the retained sets and the scanned range larger; the commit thread repeatedly rescans the whole backlog while blocking worker threads that need the same lock in add_offset()/complete_offset(). This degrades precisely under a slow-item backlog.

false_positives.candidate:
New sorted-set operations are incompatible with existing Redis segment keys

Existing span-buf:s:* keys created before this change are Redis sets, but process_spans now issues ZADD against them and the Lua script and _load_segment_data use ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN. Redis will return WRONGTYPE for those keys, so batches for traces active during deployment can fail until the keys expire after redis_ttl (3600s), and mixed old/new consumers during rollout will break each other. No key-version bump, conversion, or fallback is provided.

ZUNIONSTORE sums duplicate span scores instead of preserving timestamps

Both merge sites call ZUNIONSTORE without an AGGREGATE clause, so Redis defaults to SUM. When the same payload exists in both the destination and source sorted sets (e.g. duplicate delivery or a span stored under two keys before redirects converge), its score becomes roughly twice its end_timestamp_precise. That corrupts the ordering later used by ZPOPMIN eviction, causing duplicated spans to be retained while unrelated spans are evicted. The merge should use AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN) to preserve a real timestamp.

Insert-time eviction silently flushes incomplete segments as if complete

When a segment exceeds a hard-coded 1000 spans, ZPOPMIN discards the lowest end_timestamp_precise spans with no metric, log, or marker on the flushed segment. Those spans are permanently lost, yet flush_segments will emit the remainder as a normal segment (and the has-root flag/queue timeout may already have been set, so it flushes on the short root timeout). This replaces the previous explicit too-large-segment handling with silent partial data, ignores the configurable SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (default 1001), and with tied scores eviction order is lexicographic by payload, so even a needed span can be dropped arbitrarily.

Redirect chain resolution regresses from 10000 to 1000 hops

The loop that follows span-buf:sr redirects was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations, removing the comment that explained the 10k limit. Segment trees whose parent chain needs more than 1000 redirect hops will stop at an intermediate span ID, so later spans are merged into the wrong set and the trace is flushed as multiple split segments instead of one segment. No test or justification covers chains between 1000 and 10000 hops.

Flush-time max_segment_spans protection was removed without an equivalent guard

_load_segment_data no longer checks len(payloads[key]) against self.max_segment_spans, drops the segment_span_count_exceeded metric/log, and returns arbitrarily large segments as long as they stay under the byte limit. Segments created before the Lua eviction existed, created by mixed-version workers, or built under a different configured limit will now be loaded and produced downstream regardless of the configured span cap, risking oversized Kafka messages and memory pressure during flush.

process_batch now crashes the whole batch if end_timestamp_precise is absent

Span construction changed from tolerating minimal span payloads to requiring val["end_timestamp_precise"] via direct indexing; the cast to SpanEvent is typing-only and does not validate the runtime JSON. A single older or malformed message missing that field raises KeyError, aborting process_batch for every span in the batch and causing the same batch to be retried instead of only the bad message being dropped or defaulted.

No tests cover eviction, score merging, or the new paginator path

The added/updated tests only supply end_timestamp_precise for existing small-segment scenarios. Nothing inserts more than 1000 spans into one segment to verify how many and which spans survive ZPOPMIN, whether the root span is retained, or how duplicate payloads merged by ZUNIONSTORE keep their scores, and there are no tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator against a datetime-ordered queryset or for negative cursors. The riskiest new behaviors in this change are therefore unverified.

false_positives.candidate:
Upsampling cache can return stale or colliding eligibility results

Eligibility is cached for 60 seconds under a key containing only organization ID and hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))). The defined invalidate_upsampling_cache helper is never called when the project allowlist option changes, so projects removed from the allowlist can continue to be overcounted and newly added projects can continue to be undercounted until expiry; a hash collision between different project sets would also reuse the wrong eligibility. The TTL can additionally expire between the multiple _get_event_stats calls made by the dashboard-split flow, producing inconsistent transformations within one request.

Substring event.type check misclassifies discover queries in both directions

_is_error_focused_query only searches request.GET['query'] for the substring 'event.type:error'. A negated query such as '!event.type:error' therefore returns True and applies sum(sample_weight) to non-error events, while valid error-focused forms such as '!event.type:transaction', 'event.type:[error,default]', or the errors-only split query constructed by the endpoint ('(<query>) AND !event.type:transaction') return False because the helper also ignores the actual query argument passed to _get_event_stats. This causes overcounting for excluded-error queries and missed upsampling for legitimate error queries.

upsampled_count has no fallback for events without sample_weight

The aggregate is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)), replacing a row count that counted every event. Any stored error row whose sample_weight is null or 0 (for example events ingested before client sampling was enabled/configured for an allowlisted project, or events without a client_sample_rate) contributes 0 instead of 1, so historical or unsampled buckets in the retention window can drop to zero or be undercounted after the transformation. The added tests only cover events explicitly given client_sample_rate through the new factory helper.

upsampled_count is exposed as a public Discover function

The new SnQLFunction does not set private=True, unlike internal-only aggregates, so it becomes user-callable through the Discover query builder. A caller can submit upsampled_count() directly as a yAxis/field for projects and datasets that never passed the organization-events-stats allowlist and dataset checks, bypassing the gating in error_upsampling.py and receiving raw sum(sample_weight) results (including misleading zero values for transaction data).

It is unrelated to the upsampling feature and will change checkout/CI behavior for every developer by introducing a nested Sentry checkout; it should be removed before merging.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial key uses raw subject identifier and ambiguous underscore concatenation

permDenialKey is built from checkReq.UserUID, the raw identifier parsed from the subject, whereas permCache is keyed by the canonical UID returned by GetUserIdentifiers. The same person addressed as user:<numeric-id> versus user:<uid> therefore gets separate denial entries and inconsistent fast-path behaviour. Additionally userPermDenialCacheKey joins action, name and parent with '_' without escaping, so pairs such as (name='a_b', parent='c') and (name='a', parent='b_c') produce the same key and one resource's denial can incorrectly deny the other for that user.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says userPermDenialCacheKey joins components with '_' without escaping. It gives a concrete collision example where one resource's denial wrongly applies to another. This is the same issue as the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key does not include identity type

userPermDenialCacheKey is built only from namespace, the raw subject identifier, action, name and parent. Anonymous subjects (anonymous:0) and the render service (render:0) both have identifier "0", and user/service-account identifiers can also overlap. If an anonymous check for dashboards:read on dash1 is denied and cached, a subsequent render-service check for the same action/name/parent hits that denial at service.go:117 and returns Allowed=false, even though getRendererPermissions grants the renderer read access to all dashboards/folders. Different identity types must not share denial entries; include the identity type (or identity-specific prefixes like the permission cache uses) in the key.

Every distinct cache-negative Check now issues a fresh permissions DB query

When cached permissions do not allow the request, Check unconditionally calls getIdentityPermissions, and getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions no longer consult permCache before querying permissionStore. The denial cache is per user+action+name+parent, so it only suppresses repeats for the exact same resource. Checking N different dashboards/folders a user cannot access (e.g. an authorizer evaluating many objects, or a client probing/enumerating UIDs) therefore causes N sequential SQL permission queries for the same user/action, even though the scope map was already fetched and refreshed by the first query; singleflight only coalesces concurrent identical calls. This defeats the 30s permission cache for denial-heavy workloads and amplifies DB load proportional to distinct resource names.

Cached denial blocks access immediately after a grant or resource creation

Any DB-confirmed denial is stored in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30s), and lines 116-121 return that denial without re-querying permissions. If the denied check happened just before the resource was created or before a permission/role was granted for that same name/parent (a common pre-creation or permission-assignment flow), the creator/grantee is still denied for up to 30s, which is exactly the newly-created dashboard/folder scenario this PR aims to fix. The denial timestamp also starts after the underlying permission/team/role caches were populated, so it can extend staleness beyond their expiry.

List still serves stale cached permissions, so newly created resources do not appear

List returns getCachedIdentityPermissions whenever the cache lookup succeeds, with no revalidation, freshness check, or DB fallback. If a user creates a dashboard/folder (adding a permission not present in the cached scope map) and then lists dashboards/folders within the 30s permCache TTL, the new resource is omitted from the List response even though a Check for that same resource would now re-query the DB and allow it. This leaves Check and List inconsistent and does not fully deliver the stated goal of letting users fetch newly created dashboards/folders.

DB fallback does not refresh team, basic-role or folder-tree caches before caching a denial

The fallback at lines 139-155 re-queries only the permission rows: getUserPermissions still obtains basic role and team memberships from basicRoleCache/teamCache, and the second checkPermission still obtains ancestors from the cached folderCache via buildFolderTree. If access should be granted because of a recent team/role change or via a newly created intermediate folder, the fallback still evaluates with the stale role/team/folder-tree data, returns false, and then writes a fresh 30s denial entry, extending the incorrect denial beyond the expiry of those underlying caches. Re-querying permissions alone is insufficient for inherited or role/team-based grants.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the Integration.DoesNotExist branch immediately returns pipeline.next_step() without comparing the pipeline's github_authenticated_user to the user who installed the GitHub app. Creation of the Integration row by the GitHub webhook is asynchronous and can race or be missed, so an attacker who knows or guesses a victim's incremental GitHub installation_id and starts the linking flow before that row exists can finish the pipeline; build_integration then creates/links the integration based only on installation_id. false_positives.candidate:
Update invalidation compares an organization-aware wrapped model against a raw model

update() obtains the original via getById(), which returns createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(): for an IdP linked to an organization its isEnabled() is overridden to also require the organization (and the organization feature) to be enabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() then evaluates getLoginPredicate() on that wrapped original but on the raw updated model, while the JPA getForLogin query that populated the cache filters on the raw enabled flag. Example: an enabled, public IdP of a disabled organization is in the cached login list (raw enabled=true), but the wrapped original reports isEnabled()=false; disabling the IdP (updated enabled=false) makes both predicates false, so no login-cache invalidation is registered and the stale internal id remains in the cached getForLogin result, violating the contract that getForLogin returns only enabled login IdPs.

Shared getLoginPredicate() semantics changed to exclude private organization brokers

LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() is a public SPI predicate previously defined purely by the LoginFilter values (enabled, not link-only, not hidden on login, matching getLoginSearchOptions()). This change additionally requires any organization-linked IdP to have kc.org.broker.public=true. That silently changes the meaning for every existing caller of the predicate, not just the new cache-invalidation code: a private organization broker that is legitimately usable once its organization is known (e.g. after organization identification) is now classified as never available for login, and the predicate no longer corresponds to the LoginFilter enum documented as containing all fields considered for login availability. The broker-public check should be local to the cache-invalidation decision instead of redefining the shared predicate.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy SQL-command entry point is not explicitly disabled

UnmarshalSQLCommand still constructs a SQLCommand through NewSQLCommand without any disabled/feature check. The newer ExpressionQueryReader is explicitly described as not yet replacing the existing transform.go query path, so this legacy path remains reachable. It is currently blocked only incidentally because sql.TablesList calls the new stub DB and fails, which is then reported as a generic invalid-SQL BadRequest. If the stub DB is later implemented or replaced, this entry point would re-enable SQL execution without passing through the reader's kill-switch and could re-expose the DuckDB RCE/LFI surface. Reject SQL explicitly in UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand, or in the service pipeline builder, with the same disabled/not-implemented error used by the reader.

The change adds an early rejection for QueryTypeSQL and stubs out the SQL DB in pkg/expr/sql/db.go, but no test files are changed. There is therefore no regression test proving a SQL expression is rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, and no updated/skipped coverage for the existing SQL parser/command tests whose TablesList/QueryFramesInto calls now always return 'not implemented'. Add tests for the disabled behavior on both query-parsing entry points and update or explicitly skip the now-obsolete DuckDB-backed SQL tests so CI demonstrates the CVE fix rather than merely failing or silently losing coverage.

The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock

GetWebAssets releases the read lock before acquiring the write lock, but never rechecks entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring it. Every goroutine that observed a nil cache during a cold start will therefore serialize on the write lock and repeat the manifest file read and parsing, overwriting the cache each time, while the exclusive lock also blocks fast-path readers for the duration of that I/O. On a burst of concurrent index requests at startup this defeats the cache for that burst and unnecessarily serializes disk I/O; recheck the cache inside the write lock (respecting Dev mode) and return the already-loaded value when another goroutine populated it.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same flaw in GetWebAssets: the double-checked locking is incomplete because the cache is not re-checked after the write lock is acquired.

false_positives.candidate:
No concurrent regression test exercises the claimed race fix

This change adds mutex synchronization around entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines. Sequential tests would not have triggered the original data race under the race detector, so removing or misplacing one of the new lock operations in the future would not be caught. Add a same-package test that resets the global cache, serves a valid assets-manifest fixture via cfg.StaticRootPath, hammers GetWebAssets concurrently in non-Dev mode, and is run with -race.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors with full ID lists

The new cleanup paths at lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579 call r.log.Error unconditionally after successful fetches/deletes, passing a nil err and the entire ids slice (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize, e.g. 32767 IDs in the new test). Normal cleanup will therefore emit multiple huge error-level log lines per batch per annotation type, flooding logs, triggering error alerting, and masking real failures. These should be Debug-level (or removed), should not log the full ID list, and errors should only be logged where they are actually returned.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate and the golden comment raise the same issue: debugging or success information is logged at Error level, which pollutes the logs. Both suggest switching to Debug level.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Ticker change runs every cleanup job ten times more often

Changing the global cleanup ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute affects all jobs in clean(), not only annotation cleanup: expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, user invites, short URLs, and query history will also run ten times as often. This increases database and filesystem load and lock contention on every Grafana instance, is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix described in the PR, and is not documented or made configurable. The interval should be reverted to 10 minutes or separately justified and scoped to annotations only.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same issue: the cleanup ticker interval was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which raises database load and contention.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteByIDs can exceed parameter limits on non-SQLite databases

For every database except the special-cased SQLite path, deleteByIDs builds a single DELETE with one placeholder per fetched ID, and the number of IDs is bounded only by the configurable AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize. PostgreSQL and MySQL prepared statements are limited to 65535 parameters, so a larger configured batch size that previously worked with the subquery DELETE will now fail on every batch and abort cleanup. The delete should be chunked into bounded groups for all dialects rather than only working around SQLite.

SQLite ID list construction is quadratic for large batches

The SQLite branch rebuilds the IN list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside the loop, copying the entire accumulated string on every iteration. For the 32767-ID batch exercised by the new test this is O(n^2) copying (gigabytes of intermediate copying) on each affected annotation type, undermining the large-batch support the branch is meant to add. Build the list with strings.Builder or strings.Join instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Storage failures are recorded in the wrong duration metric

When Storage.Create fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration; Update has the same mistake on its storage-error path, and DeleteCollection records its asynchronous legacy result with recordStorageDuration. Storage and legacy latency/error dashboards and alerts will therefore attribute failures to the wrong backend and can hide unified-storage errors.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug pattern: storage and legacy duration metrics are swapped. The candidate explicitly flags a metric mixup in DeleteCollection, though it describes the direction somewhat differently. It also names the same pattern in Create and Update.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete uses the object name as the Prometheus kind label

The successful Delete path calls recordStorageDuration with name where the other methods pass options.Kind. Prometheus labels must be bounded; using a distinct resource name for every deleted object creates unbounded metric cardinality, increasing memory and query cost and breaking comparisons by kind. It should pass options.Kind like the error path and other methods.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same problem: Delete records metrics with name instead of options.Kind, which is inconsistent with the other methods. The candidate adds the cardinality impact, but the underlying issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and can be cancelled immediately

Create derives its 10-second legacy-write context from the incoming request context; the same pattern is used for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. Once the API handler finishes and returns the response, the request context is cancelled, so an in-flight legacy write can be aborted despite the 10-second timeout. This can silently leave legacy storage without the backup write that mode 3 is intended to provide. The context needs to be detached from request cancellation while preserving request values such as authentication.

Async legacy Create races with use of the returned object

Create passes the original obj to Legacy.Create in a goroutine after Storage.Create has returned created from that same input. Storage implementations may mutate obj or return an object aliasing it, while the caller will proceed to serialize or otherwise use created. The legacy store can therefore concurrently read or mutate shared object state, causing a data race or changing the response after unified storage has completed. The object should be deep-copied before launching the asynchronous legacy write.

Update reuses objInfo instead of propagating the unified-storage result to legacy

Update passes the same UpdatedObjectInfo independently to unified storage and then asynchronously to legacy storage, dropping the previous updateWrapper behavior. UpdatedObject will be computed a second time against legacy's old object, so the two stores can receive different content when their old objects or resource versions differ, and implementations that cache or mutate the decoded object can make the second computation incorrect. Legacy should receive the same updated object that unified storage accepted, as the previous implementation ensured.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight asynchronous legacy writes

Mode 3 launches fire-and-forget goroutines for legacy writes but keeps no WaitGroup or other tracking. Destroy immediately destroys both storages, so shutdown can terminate or close legacy storage while writes are still running, losing backup writes or causing use-after-destroy failures. Asynchronous work needs to be tracked and drained before the underlying storages are destroyed.

Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes

The new tests invoke Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection but do not wait for or assert the legacy goroutines, and both stores share one testify mock with indistinguishable expectations. The tests therefore pass even if a legacy method is never called, is called with the wrong object, or fails asynchronously after the test returns. They need synchronization and separate assertions that each legacy operation eventually runs with the expected arguments.

Mode 3 playlist integration test assumes synchronous legacy visibility

The new mode 3 integration cases reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates or updates through the Kubernetes API and immediately reads the same data through the legacy playlist API. Mode 3 now writes to legacy in a background goroutine, so there is no ordering guarantee that the legacy rows exist when those immediate assertions run. This introduces intermittent integration-test failures unless the test polls for legacy visibility or the helper waits for asynchronous writes to settle.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem. GrafanaRuleListItem is rendered in a list without a React key prop, which can cause rendering or reconciliation issues when the list order changes.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
